sharedText: in all the borders round about
reason: A genuine six-word run and the highest-ranked candidate in the chapter, but the phrase is a surveyor's formula in both places and nothing else is shared. Genesis 23:17 is the conveyance of the field of Machpelah; Alma 28:1 is a description of Nephite troop dispositions round Zarahemla. 'In all the borders' recurs at Ezekiel 45:1 in the same neutral sense. The n-gram stream is doing what CONVENTIONS §9 says it does — scoring rare boilerplate.

'Tens of thousands of the Lamanites were slain' invites the women's song of Saul's thousands and David's ten thousands, and the Book of Mormon does use that arithmetic deliberately — it is adjudicated at 1 Nephi 4:1, where 'his tens of thousands' answers Laman's objection about Laban's fifty. Here it is not doing that work: the phrase is a casualty count in a battle report, 'ten thousands' occurs in eleven KJV verses, and 'tens of thousands' in none. The reader who wants the David allusion is sent to 1 Nephi 4:1.

Tempting, and worth recording as declined rather than passed over: Alma 28:6 repeats 'a time of' twice in one clause ('a time of solemnity, and a time of much fasting and prayer'), which is the anaphora of Ecclesiastes 3:1-8. But Ecclesiastes builds its catalogue out of paired opposites and runs to fourteen members; Alma 28:6 has two members and no antithesis between them, and it shares no content word with any verse of Ecclesiastes 3. The link at this verse goes to 1 Corinthians 7:5 instead, on the order of 'fasting and prayer'.

sharedText: the fifteenth year of the reign
reason: 'The fifteenth year of the reign' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 15:10 (Asa) and Luke 3:1 (Tiberius), and the dossier ranked both at the head of this verse and of 28:9. The singleton-style rarity is an artifact of serial counting. The Book of Mormon dates by the year of the reign of the judges continuously from Alma 1:1 onward and must therefore produce every ordinal in turn; that the fifteenth happens to be one the KJV also uses twice is arithmetic, not borrowing. The regnal-dating formula itself is first used at Alma 1:1 and belongs there if it belongs anywhere.

sharedText: the fifteenth year of the reign of
reason: The same coincidence as at 28:7, where it is set out at length: a seven-word run produced by a serial year-count meeting the KJV's only two verses that name a fifteenth regnal year. Neither Asa's covenant assembly nor Tiberius's accession has any contact with this verse's summary of Nephite wars.

sharedText: upon the face of the earth
reason: Alma 28:11 contrasts bodies 'laid low in the earth' with bodies 'mouldering in heaps upon the face of the earth', which is the prophets' topos of the unburied dead after a slaughter — Ezekiel 39:11-16 detailing the burial of the multitude of Gog, and Jeremiah 8:2 and 16:4, where the slain 'shall not be gathered, nor be buried; they shall be for dung upon the face of the earth.' The topos is certainly in the background. The wording will not carry a link: 'upon the face of the earth' occurs in twelve KJV verses, 'in heaps' and 'mouldering' in none, and no candidate verse shares anything else.

sharedText: snare / taken captive by him at his will
reason: 'The cunning plans which he hath devised to ensnare the hearts of men' is the same borrowing already adjudicated in this book at Alma 12:6, where the snare of the devil of 2 Timothy 2:26 is drawn on three times in one discourse. This is the editor reusing a formula the book has already established, not a fresh contact with the source (ADJUDICATING §4), and the argument is at Alma 12:6.

The model case for why an exact-string singleton proves nothing on its own. 'In the vineyards of' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is Song of Solomon 1:14 — 'My beloved is unto me as a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi' — a lover's simile with no labour, no Lord and no vineyard-owner in it. The real sources at this verse share no exact run with it at all: Matthew 20:1's 'labourers into his vineyard' and Isaiah 5:7's 'the vineyard of the LORD of hosts', each a singleton in its own right, fused into 'labor in the vineyards of the Lord'.
